outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Case Background and Procedural History
outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of the dispute, including the technology involved (Passive Intermodulation or PIM), the specific patents at issue ('134 and '775), the parties involved, and the procedural journey from the jury verdict to the Federal Circuit appeal. It details the initial litigation strategy, the jury's finding of infringement and damages, and the specific post-trial motions (JMOL and new trial) that were denied by the district court.
subtopics: Overview of Passive Intermodulation (PIM) Technology
Identification of Patents '134 and '775 and Their Subject Matter
Parties: Finesse Wireless LLC vs. AT&T/Nokia
Procedural Posture: Jury Verdict ($166M Award) and Denial of Post-Trial Motions
Jurisdictional Basis for Appeal to the Federal Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Standard of Review for Noninfringement JMOL
outline.description: This chapter defines the legal framework applied by the Federal Circuit to evaluate whether a jury's infringement verdict should be overturned via Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL). It distinguishes between de novo review of claim construction, clear error review of factual findings, and substantive evidence review for infringement. Crucially, it outlines the stringent standard required to reverse a jury verdict in favor of noninfringement under Fifth Circuit precedent.
subtopics: Review Standards: De Novo for Construction vs. Substantial Evidence for Facts
The 'Light Most Favorable' Standard for JMOL Denials in the Fifth Circuit
Defining 'Substantial Evidence' in Patent Infringement Cases
The Burden of Proof Placed on the Patent Owner (Plaintiff)
Impact of Contradictory Expert Testimony on Sufficiency of Evidence

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Analysis of U.S. Patent No. 7,346,134 - Sampling Limitations
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep dive into the technical failure regarding Claim 1(a) of the '134 patent. It analyzes why Finesse failed to prove that its accused devices sampled both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals.' The core issue focuses on Dr. Wells' contradictory testimony regarding whether a modeled PIM path could exist prior to sampling, creating an impossible temporal sequence that rendered his opinion legally insufficient.
subtopics: '134 Patent Claim 1 Structure: Isolating Signals and Computing Estimates
Critical Limitation 1(a): The Requirement to Sample Both Signal Types Simultaneously
Expert Testimony Analysis: Mapping Signals to x1/x2 vs. Modeled PIM Path
,The Temporal Impossibility Argument: Can You Sample What Hasn't Been Generated?
->Evaluation of Conflicting Expert Testimony as Insufficient Evidence for JMOL Reversal

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Analysis of U.S. Patent No. 9,548,775 - Multiplication Requirements
outline.description: This chapter examines the infringement analysis for Claim 1(d) of the '775 patent, focusing on two main issues: whether three signals must be unique inputs versus separate identifiers, and whether the accused device performs seven distinct multiplications rather than three. It discusses prosecution history estoppel arguments regarding claim amendments and evaluates why Dr. Wells' mapping theory failed due to lack of evidence connecting actual device operations to every claimed multiplication.
subtopics: '775 Patent Claim Structure: Seven Third-Order Multiplications Methodology
Claim Construction Debate:'Separately Identifiable'Signals vs.'Unique'Inputs
Prosecution History Estoppel Did Not Disclaim Two-Signal Embodiments
Evidence Gap:Nokia Documents Show Three Distinct Operations Not Seven
Inability to Map Complex Conjugates/Modulus Operations to Claimed S1/S2/S3 Products

outline.description: This chapter explains why damages were vacated once noninfringement was established across all claims. It briefly covers the appellate standard for reviewing denials of new trials on damages but emphasizes that without a valid basis for infringement liability, any damage calculation becomes moot. The chapter concludes with the final disposition ordering costs back to Appellants.
subtopics: Relationship Between Infringement Finding and Damage Awards
Standard for New Trial Motions on Damages
Effect of Total Reversal on Liability
